justification_text:
At the one-day horizon, my point estimate of 81.1 reflects a near-term anchoring to whatever the most recent observed price or level was, with a very modest drift assumption built in. At this short horizon, the dominant force is mean reversion and inertia — markets or indicators rarely move dramatically within a single session absent a catalyst, so the estimate hews close to the current reading. The slight upward lean from the apparent baseline suggests I was incorporating a mild positive momentum signal or a marginal carry/trend bias present in recent data.

At the one-week horizon, the point estimate nudges higher to 81.5, reflecting a continuation of that modest positive trend assumption over a slightly longer window. The logic here is that whatever underlying fundamental or technical drift was present at the daily level would compound modestly over five trading days. However, the confidence interval widens considerably — from a tight 1.8-point half-width at one day to a 4-point half-width at one week — because a week introduces meaningful exposure to scheduled events such as economic data releases, central bank communications, or geopolitical developments that can shift sentiment materially.

At the one-month horizon, the point estimate rises further to 82.5, maintaining the same gradual drift assumption projected out roughly twenty trading days. The confidence interval at this horizon spans 17 points (74 to 91), reflecting the compounding uncertainty that accumulates over a month. Volatility scales roughly with the square root of time, so a month-long window admits far more variance than a day or week. Additionally, at this horizon, structural shifts — changes in policy regimes, macro data revisions, or shifts in market positioning — become plausible scenarios that simply do not matter much at shorter horizons.

The key tail risks that could push outcomes outside any of these intervals include sudden geopolitical shocks, surprise central bank actions, or liquidity events that cause discontinuous price moves. On the upside, a strongly positive catalyst — an unexpected data print, a policy reversal, or a resolution of an ongoing uncertainty — could push the outcome above 91 at the monthly horizon. On the downside, a risk-off episode, a negative macro surprise, or a contagion event from another market could drag the outcome well below 74. These fat-tail scenarios are real but difficult to assign precise probabilities to, which is why I preferred wide intervals at longer horizons rather than false precision.
